summary: For learners aged 8–11, teach the shift from 'make something' to DEFINING a design problem before building: name the user, state measurable success criteria, and list real constraints (materials, time, cost, size). The core skills are (1) rewriting vague wishes ('make it good/strong') into testable criteria ('holds 500 g without bending'; 'the cup holds 200 ml without leaking for one minute'), (2) distinguishing a criterion (a goal the solution must meet) from a constraint (a limit on how you may reach it), and (3) keeping in problem-space instead of jumping to a favourite solution. There is no single 'right' brief — a good brief is a defensible one that makes success checkable. The main activity has learners author a full design brief for an authentic, bounded need; supporting activities sort and sharpen individual statements; alternatives use annotated worked briefs and in-role client interviews to elicit and explain these distinctions.
misconceptions: Treating vague wishes as criteria ("make it nice/good/strong") instead of measurable outcomes.
Confusing criteria (goals) with constraints (limits) — e.g. listing 'use only card' as a success criterion.
Jumping straight to a favourite solution and back-filling the problem to fit it.
Thinking there is one 'right' problem statement, rather than a defensible one that makes success checkable.
Ignoring the user — writing criteria for what the maker wants, not what the named user needs.

activities.title: Author a design brief for a real, named user
steps: Choose a bounded, authentic need with a named user — for example 'a younger child needs to carry three library books across the playground in the rain', or 'the reading corner gets so bright in the afternoon that children can't read the tablet screens' — and write the NEED in problem terms.

Write at least two SUCCESS CRITERIA, phrased so you could actually check them. For each, ask 'How would we SEE or MEASURE this?' Rewrite 'make it strong' as 'holds 500 g without bending' and 'make it good' as an observable condition.
List at least one real CONSTRAINT on materials, time, or cost (e.g. 'only card and tape', 'one afternoon', 'under £2'), and say what option that constraint rules out.
Spend the whole session only defining the problem — do NOT design or build a solution yet.
Check your own brief: could someone use it to judge whether a finished solution worked? If a criterion can't be checked, rewrite it.
activities.insight: Defining a problem is itself a distinct act of construction: a good brief turns a vague wish into something whose success you could actually check, names who it is for, and states the limits you must work within — before any building begins. There is no single correct brief, only a defensible one that makes success checkable.

activities.title: Sort statements: criterion or constraint?
steps: Take a mixed set of about eight statements (some success goals, some limits on materials/time/cost) and sort each into two columns: CRITERIA (what success looks like) vs CONSTRAINTS (a limit you must work within).
For each placement, say in one sentence why it belongs there — e.g. 'use only card' is a limit on how you work, so it's a constraint.
For any statement you got wrong on a first pass, explain what made it easy to mix up.
activities.insight: A criterion is a goal the solution must meet; a constraint is a limit on how you may reach it. The same brief needs both, and they play different roles.

activities.title: Make it testable: rewrite vague criteria and set a threshold
steps: Given a vague criterion such as 'make it strong', rewrite it as a measurable statement (e.g. 'holds 500 g without bending').
Given a need, choose a reasonable success threshold and justify it (e.g. 'the cup must hold 200 ml without leaking for one minute').
Given two phrasings of the same criterion, pick the one you could actually check and say why the other can't be tested.
activities.insight: A criterion is only useful if someone could observe or measure whether it was met; naming a quantity, time, or observable condition is what makes a wish testable. (The source requires criteria to be 'specified'; making them observable is how we meet that at this age.)

activities.title: Interview the client to sharpen the brief
steps: Take on the role of a designer talking to the named user (the 'client') about their need.
Ask the client questions and let the client keep pushing back with 'How would we KNOW it worked?' until each proposed criterion becomes measurable.
After the conversation, write down the agreed need, two or more measurable criteria, and at least one constraint the client named (budget, time, or materials).
activities.insight: Problem-definition is a questioning stance: good criteria emerge by repeatedly asking how success would be checked and listening to what the user actually needs.

activities.title: Unpack a worked design brief
steps: Read a complete, well-formed design brief for a named user (need, user, criteria, constraints).
For each criterion, explain why it is measurable — what you could observe or measure to check it.
For each constraint, explain what option it rules out of the solution space.
Then write one new criterion and one new constraint you think the brief is missing, keeping them testable and real.
activities.insight: Seeing a strong brief dissected shows what 'measurable' and 'limiting' look like concretely, giving a model to imitate when writing your own — and the brief you add to is one defensible version, not the only possible one.

checkQuestion: The reading corner gets so bright in the afternoon that children can't see the tablet screens. Before anyone builds anything, I want you to define the design problem: write down what need it addresses, at least two things a good solution must do (so we could tell if it worked), and what would limit us — like materials, time, or money. (Set the scenario and watch how the child frames it; do not supply the criteria yourself.)
checkAnswer: The child states the need in problem terms (reduce glare on the screens in the reading corner), specifies at least two success criteria phrased so you could check them (e.g. 'the screen is readable at 2 pm', 'it doesn't make the corner too dark to read a book'), and identifies real constraints — available materials, time, cost, or that it mustn't block the walkway — all WITHOUT jumping to a particular solution.
